course.title: Sound and Audio Fundamentals
course.description: What sound is, how we hear it, how it is measured and stored, and the principles behind shaping it: decibels, spectrum, sampling, compression, EQ, reverb and sound design.
course.audience: A curious adult with school-level maths and physics who makes or wants to make audio for games, video or music, or simply wants to know why sound behaves as it does. No software or hardware needed; the course teaches concepts, and tools appear only as current examples.

paragraphs: A struck tuning fork makes a pure tone, and that tone can be described completely by two numbers: how many times a second the air pressure at your ear rises and falls, and how far it swings each time. Add the speed at which the pattern travels, about 343 metres a second in air, and a great deal follows by arithmetic, from the length of a bass note's wave, which is longer than most rooms, to the note a pipe of a given length will sound.

Sound becomes a richer subject once you include the listener, because the ear is not a measuring instrument. It hears equal ratios of frequency as equal steps of pitch, it is far more sensitive at some frequencies than at others, and a loud sound can hide a quieter one close to it in frequency. Those facts about hearing decide how much of a pressure wave a recording has to keep, which is why music streamed at a tenth of a CD's data rate can sound the same to most listeners.

Put the physics and the hearing together and you can reason about sound with numbers. You can say how much quieter a source becomes at twice the distance, which frequencies a given sample rate can hold, how far a compressor will turn down a drum hit, and how long a room will keep ringing after a clap.
outcomes: You'll be able to relate frequency, wavelength, period and the speed of sound.
You'll be able to read a spectrum and explain timbre through harmonics.
You'll be able to calculate with decibels, including level changes from doubling distance or adding sources.
You'll be able to explain how hearing limits what we perceive and how masking enables lossy compression.
You'll be able to compute sampling limits, aliasing, bit-depth ranges and file sizes.
You'll be able to predict what a compressor, filter or reverb does to a signal.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Maths Foundations, Physics: Motion and Forces.

modules.title: The physics of sound
modules.description: Sound as a wave, and the quantities that describe it: speed, frequency, wavelength, harmonics and resonance.

modules.title: Hearing and measurement
modules.description: How the ear responds and how the decibel scale describes level.

modules.title: Digital audio
modules.description: How a continuous wave becomes numbers and what is lost or kept in storage.

modules.title: Shaping sound
modules.description: Dynamics, filters, reverb and the principles of designing a sound.

concepts.title: Sound wave
concepts.summary: A sound wave is a travelling pattern of compressions and rarefactions in a medium, produced by a vibrating source.

concepts.title: Longitudinal wave
concepts.summary: In a longitudinal wave the particles move back and forth along the direction in which the wave travels.

concepts.title: Speed of sound
concepts.summary: The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature, not on loudness or pitch; in air at 20 C it is about 343 m/s.

concepts.title: Medium
concepts.summary: Sound needs matter to travel through, so it cannot propagate in a vacuum.

concepts.title: Frequency
concepts.summary: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, in hertz, and it sets the pitch heard.

concepts.title: Period
concepts.summary: The period is the time of one cycle, T = 1 / f.

concepts.title: Wavelength
concepts.summary: Wavelength is the distance over which a wave repeats, and v = f x wavelength.

concepts.title: Amplitude
concepts.summary: Amplitude is the size of the pressure variation and sets the loudness, not the pitch.

concepts.title: Phase
concepts.summary: Phase is the position within a cycle; two waves offset by half a cycle can cancel.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.summary: A spectrum plots the amplitude of each frequency component of a sound.

concepts.title: Harmonic series
concepts.summary: The harmonics of a note with fundamental f are f, 2f, 3f, 4f and so on.

concepts.title: Timbre
concepts.summary: Timbre is the quality that separates two sounds of equal pitch and loudness, and depends largely on the relative amplitudes of the harmonics.

concepts.title: Fourier analysis
concepts.summary: Any steady periodic wave can be built by adding sine waves at the harmonics of its frequency.

concepts.title: Standard waveshapes
concepts.summary: A square wave has only odd harmonics with amplitude 1/n; a sawtooth has all harmonics with amplitude 1/n.

concepts.title: Standing wave
concepts.summary: A standing wave forms when waves reflect between ends and interfere, leaving nodes of no motion and antinodes of maximum motion.

concepts.title: String modes
concepts.summary: A string fixed at both ends has frequencies f_n = n v / (2L).

concepts.title: Open pipe
concepts.summary: An open pipe has f_n = n v / (2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, ... (ideal pipe, end corrections ignored).

concepts.title: Closed pipe
concepts.summary: A pipe closed at one end has f_n = n v / (4L) with only odd n.

concepts.title: Resonance
concepts.summary: Resonance is a large response of a system driven near one of its natural frequencies.

concepts.title: Path through the ear
concepts.summary: Sound passes the pinna and ear canal to the eardrum, through three small bones (malleus, incus and stapes) to the cochlea, where hair cells convert vibration to nerve signals.

concepts.title: Range of hearing
concepts.summary: Young healthy ears hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, a span of about 10 octaves, and the upper limit falls with age and noise damage.

concepts.title: Ear-canal resonance
concepts.summary: The ear canal acts like a pipe closed at one end and boosts sound around 3 kHz, where the ear is most sensitive.

concepts.title: Equal-loudness contours
concepts.summary: Equal-loudness contours show that tones of different frequency need different pressure levels to sound equally loud, with greatest sensitivity at 2 to 5 kHz.

concepts.title: Logarithmic pitch
concepts.summary: Equal frequency ratios are heard as equal pitch intervals, so an octave is always a 2:1 ratio.

concepts.title: Decibel
concepts.summary: The decibel is ten times the base-10 logarithm of a power ratio, so every factor of 10 in power is 10 dB.

concepts.title: Sound pressure level
concepts.summary: SPL = 20 log10(p / p0) with p0 = 20 micropascals, the nominal threshold of hearing at 1 kHz, which is 0 dB SPL.

concepts.title: Doubling rules
concepts.summary: Doubling power adds 3.01 dB and doubling pressure adds 6.02 dB.

concepts.title: Inverse-square law
concepts.summary: For a point source in free space, intensity falls with the square of distance, so each doubling of distance lowers the level by 6.02 dB.

concepts.title: Exposure limits
concepts.summary: Safe-listening guidance sets 85 dBA for 8 hours and halves the time for every 3 dB more.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.summary: Sampling measures the signal's amplitude at equal time steps, and the sample rate is the number of measurements per second.

concepts.title: Nyquist frequency
concepts.summary: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate, and a sampled signal can represent only frequencies below it.

concepts.title: Aliasing
concepts.summary: A tone above the Nyquist frequency folds back and appears at |f - fs| (for fs/2 < f < fs), so it cannot be told from a lower real tone.

concepts.title: Anti-aliasing filter
concepts.summary: A low-pass filter before the converter removes content above the Nyquist frequency before sampling.

concepts.title: Reconstruction
concepts.summary: A band-limited signal sampled above twice its highest frequency can be rebuilt exactly.

concepts.title: Quantisation
concepts.summary: Quantisation rounds each sample to one of 2^N levels, where N is the bit depth, and the rounding error is heard as noise.

concepts.title: Dynamic range
concepts.summary: For an ideal quantiser with a full-scale sine the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio is 6.02 N + 1.76 dB, about 6 dB per bit.

concepts.title: Data rate
concepts.summary: Uncompressed data rate is sample rate x bit depth x number of channels.

concepts.title: Dither
concepts.summary: Dither adds a very small noise before quantising so that quantisation error is not correlated with the signal.

concepts.title: Clipping
concepts.summary: A signal beyond full scale cannot be represented and is flattened, which adds harmonics.

concepts.title: Lossless compression
concepts.summary: Lossless compression stores the same samples in fewer bits and decodes to an exact copy.

concepts.title: Lossy compression
concepts.summary: Lossy compression discards information that listeners are expected not to miss, so the decoded signal differs from the original.

concepts.title: Masking
concepts.summary: A loud sound makes nearby frequencies, or the instants just before and after it, inaudible at a lower level.

concepts.title: Bitrate
concepts.summary: Bitrate is the data per second of the stored stream, and for a lossy codec it is chosen directly.

concepts.title: Generation loss
concepts.summary: Each lossy encode of already lossy audio throws away more, so editing masters should be uncompressed.

concepts.title: Envelope
concepts.summary: The envelope of a sound is how its amplitude changes in time, commonly described by attack, decay, sustain and release.

concepts.title: Compressor
concepts.summary: Above its threshold a compressor lets the output rise by only 1 dB for every R dB the input rises, where R is the ratio.

concepts.title: Gain reduction
concepts.summary: Gain reduction is the input level minus the output level, in dB.

concepts.title: Limiter
concepts.summary: A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio, used to stop the level exceeding a ceiling.

concepts.title: Loudness measurement
concepts.summary: Loudness is measured in LUFS, a weighted level over time, to compare programmes whatever their peaks.

concepts.title: Filter types
concepts.summary: Low-pass filters pass frequencies below a cutoff, high-pass above it, band-pass within a range, and shelves raise or cut everything above or below a corner.

concepts.title: Cutoff frequency
concepts.summary: The cutoff is where the response has fallen 3 dB from the passband.

concepts.title: Slope
concepts.summary: A filter's slope is its attenuation per octave: each filter order adds about 6 dB per octave.

concepts.title: Q factor
concepts.summary: Q is centre frequency divided by bandwidth, so a narrow band has a high Q.

concepts.title: Equalisation
concepts.summary: Equalisation raises or cuts bands to correct a sound or to make space for others in a mix.

concepts.title: Reverberation
concepts.summary: Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a space as many reflections arrive after the direct sound.

concepts.title: RT60
concepts.summary: RT60 is the time for the sound level to fall by 60 dB after the source stops.

concepts.title: Sabine equation
concepts.summary: RT60 = 0.161 V / A seconds, with V the room volume in cubic metres and A the total absorption in square metres (sabins).

concepts.title: Early reflections
concepts.summary: Reflections arriving within about 50 ms of the direct sound fuse with it and tell the ear about room size.

concepts.title: Precedence effect
concepts.summary: When two similar sounds arrive within a few milliseconds to about 30 ms, the ear localises to the first arrival.

concepts.title: Layering
concepts.summary: Layering builds a sound from several parts, such as an attack transient, a body and a low tail, each occupying its own range.

concepts.title: Speed and pitch
concepts.summary: Playing a recording faster by ratio r raises its frequencies by r and shortens its duration to 1/r; n semitones is a ratio of 2^(n/12).

concepts.title: Distance cues
concepts.summary: Distant sounds are quieter, duller (air absorbs highs), and have more reverberation relative to direct sound.

concepts.title: Doppler shift
concepts.summary: A source moving toward a listener at speed vs has observed frequency f x v / (v - vs); away, f x v / (v + vs).

concepts.title: Diegetic and non-diegetic sound
concepts.summary: Diegetic sound belongs to the story world; non-diegetic sound, such as a score, does not.

lessons.title: Sound as pressure waves

reveal.text: A candle placed between the speaker and your ear does not lean towards you, which already rules out a moving stream of air. The next screen shows what does move.

lead.text: When the speaker cone moves forward it pushes the layer of air in front of it, squeezing those particles closer together than usual. That layer pushes on the next, and so on outwards, while the cone swings back and leaves the air beside it thinner than before. A region where the air is squeezed together, with its pressure above the surrounding level, is called a **compression**, and a region where it is spread out, with pressure below that level, is called a **rarefaction**. A **sound wave** is a train of compressions and rarefactions moving away from the source, and the figure shows one row of air at three moments.

afterFigure.text: Follow the highlighted particle first. In all three views it stays near the same place, moving a short way to the right and then the same way to the left, because it only passes its push to its neighbour and is then pushed back itself. Now follow the dashed green line, which marks a compression and moves a quarter of a wavelength between one view and the next. The compression is *not* a particle: it is a place where particles are crowded, carried forward by different particles in turn.

Because the particles move along the same line as the wave travels, this kind of wave is called a **longitudinal wave**. A wave on a rope is different, since the rope moves at right angles to the direction the wave travels, but in air the motion is always back and forth along the way the sound is going.

diagram.alt: A row of air particles at three moments with the pressure curve beneath. The compression, marked by a dashed line, moves to the right between views. The highlighted particle stays near the same place, moving only a short way back and forth.
diagram.caption: The same row of air at three moments. Watch the highlighted particle, then the dashed line. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: The opposite region, where the curve dips below the dashed line, is the rarefaction. A sound wave alternates between the two as it passes any point.

lead.text: A compression can form only if there is something to squeeze, so sound needs matter to travel through, called its **medium**. Air, water and steel are all media, while a vacuum is not, and this is why sound cannot cross empty space. The speed at which the pattern advances is the **speed of sound**, and it depends on the medium: in air at 20 °C it is about 343 m/s, and in water it is about 1,480 m/s, because water particles are far harder to squeeze and push their neighbours back more quickly.

afterFigure.text: The speed does *not* depend on how loud the sound is or on its pitch. A louder sound has larger pressure changes, but the pattern still advances at the same rate, and a shout and a whisper reach the far side of a field together.

diagram.alt: Horizontal bars for the speed of sound: air at 20 degrees Celsius 343 metres per second, water about 1,480 metres per second, and a vacuum with no bar because sound cannot travel there.
diagram.caption: Speed of sound in two media, drawn to scale. A vacuum has nothing to carry the wave.

lead.text: Light crosses a few kilometres in a few millionths of a second, so for a storm the flash can be taken as instant, and the delay before the thunder is the time the sound took.

reveal.text: Each second of delay adds about 343 m, so a three-second gap puts the strike roughly a kilometre away.

steps.headline: An echo is timed from a clap to its return, which is 0.40 s here. Find the distance to the wall.

workedSteps.text: The sound has to reach the wall and come back, so the delay covers the path twice. First find the total distance the sound travelled, using 343 m/s.
This total is out and back, so the wall is half of it away.
Work out the division to give the distance to the wall, and check that it makes sense: the sound covered about 137 m in under half a second, which is possible at 343 m/s.

lead.text: Warmer air has faster-moving particles, which pass a push along sooner, so the speed of sound in air depends on temperature. Over the range of everyday weather the speed is about 331 + 0.6T metres per second, where T is the air temperature in degrees Celsius. At 20 °C it gives 331 + 0.6 × 20 = 343 m/s, the value used so far.

afterFigure.text: The change is modest, about 10% between −20 °C and 40 °C, so the 343 m/s figure is a good working value for most calculations.

diagram.caption: Speed of sound in air against temperature. It rises by about 0.6 m/s for each degree.

steps.headline: The thunder arrives 3.0 s after the flash on a day at −10 °C. Find the distance to the strike.

workedSteps.text: Start with the speed of sound at this temperature, using 331 + 0.6T.
The light is effectively instant, so the whole delay is the travel time of the sound. Multiply the speed by the delay and give the distance.

reveal.text: A ship with a fast echo sounder can repeat this many times a second, building up a profile of the sea floor from the delays alone.

lessons.orientation: What a sound wave is, how fast it travels, and how a delay in a sound gives a distance.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson describes a wave by how often it repeats and how long each repeat is, which is what pitch and wavelength measure.

blocks.text: When a speaker plays a note, its cone moves forward and back by a fraction of a millimetre, and yet someone across the room hears it. Nothing solid crosses the room, and the air that touched the cone does not travel to the listener either. What does cross is a disturbance, and it takes a measurable time: in a thunderstorm the flash arrives effectively at once and the thunder several seconds later, and the gap tells you how far away the lightning struck.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what travels when sound crosses a room, and use the speed of sound to turn a delay into a distance.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in the course, from pitch to reverb, describes some feature of this one pressure wave.

recap.keyIdea: Sound is a pattern of compressions and rarefactions that travels through a medium at a speed the medium sets, so a delay times that speed gives a distance.

blocks.text: The air carries a sound wave without travelling itself: each particle moves a little back and forth, and the pattern of crowded and spread-out regions is what moves on. In air at 20 °C that pattern advances at about 343 m/s, and the speed rises by roughly 0.6 m/s for each degree of warmth.
Because the speed is fixed by the medium, a delay between a sound and its cause measures a distance, once for a one-way trip like thunder and halved for an echo, which travels out and back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson describes a wave by how often it repeats and how long each repeat is, which is what pitch and wavelength measure.

lessons.title: Frequency, wavelength and amplitude

reveal.text: The number of complete repeats per second is the quantity the next screen names and measures in hertz.

lead.text: A steady tone shows up in a pressure record as a shape that repeats, and one complete repeat is called a **cycle**. The number of cycles in each second is the **frequency**, measured in **hertz** (Hz), so a tone of 250 Hz goes through 250 cycles every second. The time that one cycle takes is the **period**, and since 250 cycles fill one second, each of them lasts 1 / 250 s, which is 0.004 s or 4 ms.

afterFigure.text: That reciprocal link, T = 1 / f, holds for every tone: a higher frequency means a shorter period, so doubling the frequency to 500 Hz halves the period to 2 ms.

diagram.alt: Pressure plotted against time for a tone. At 250 hertz one cycle takes 4 milliseconds and three cycles fit in 12 milliseconds. At 500 hertz one cycle takes 2 milliseconds and six cycles fit.
diagram.caption: Pressure against time at the same microphone. Use the buttons to double the frequency and watch the cycle shorten.

reveal.text: A period of 10 ms is long enough that a very low note can be followed cycle by cycle on a trace.

lead.text: The height of the pressure peaks above and below the resting pressure is the wave’s **amplitude**, and it sets how loud the sound is: larger pressure variations are heard as louder sound. Frequency and amplitude are independent.

afterFigure.text: A quiet and a loud tone at 440 Hz therefore have the same **pitch**, which is how high or low a note sounds and follows the frequency, and they differ only in loudness.

diagram.alt: Three pressure traces. The original tone is 250 hertz with peaks of 1 unit. Doubling the amplitude makes the peaks twice as tall with the same spacing. Doubling the frequency keeps the height and halves the spacing.
diagram.caption: Amplitude changes the height of the peaks and frequency changes their spacing. Use the buttons to change one at a time.

reveal.text: Amplitude decides loudness, so it stays out of this question, and a note keeps its pitch as it fades away.

lead.text: If you could freeze a sound wave and plot its pressure along the direction of travel, you would see the same repeating shape as in the time trace, but spread over distance. The length of one repeat is the **wavelength**, usually written with the Greek letter λ (lambda) in physics books. In one period the wave advances one wavelength, so the speed is the wavelength divided by the period, and since 1 / T is the frequency, **v = f × wavelength**.

afterFigure.text: All frequencies travel at the same speed in a given medium, so a higher frequency can only be fitted in by making the wavelength shorter. At 343 m/s a 440 Hz tone has a wavelength of 343 / 440 = 0.78 m, and doubling the frequency to 880 Hz halves it to 0.39 m. The wavelength is the length of one repeat along the direction of travel, not the height of the wave, which is the amplitude.

The audible range stretches over a factor of 1,000 in frequency, so it does the same in wavelength: 20 Hz gives 343 / 20 = 17.15 m, while 20,000 Hz gives 343 / 20,000 = 0.01715 m, under 2 cm. Bass sounds are therefore as long as a room, and treble sounds as short as a fingertip.

diagram.alt: Pressure plotted against distance for tones in air. At 440 hertz one wavelength is 0.78 metres, so a little over two fit in 1.6 metres. At 880 hertz it is 0.39 metres, and four fit.
diagram.caption: Pressure against distance at one instant. Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Find the wavelength of a 262 Hz tone, close to middle C, in air at 20 °C.

workedSteps.text: Write the relation between speed, frequency and wavelength.
Rearrange it to give the wavelength, by dividing both sides by the frequency.
Substitute the speed in air, 343 m/s, and the frequency, 262 Hz.
Work out the division, and round to two decimal places.

steps.headline: Find the wavelength of a 5,000 Hz tone in air at 20 °C, in centimetres.

workedSteps.text: The same relation applies, with the frequency now 5,000 Hz.
Dividing gives the wavelength in metres, and 1 m is 100 cm.
Convert that length to centimetres.

lead.text: Two waves of the same frequency can differ in where they are within their cycles, a difference called **phase**. When they rise and fall together they are *in phase*, and the pressures add, so the sum has twice the peak of either wave. If the second is delayed by half a cycle, its peaks fall exactly where the first has troughs, and the sum is zero at every moment.

afterFigure.text: Cancelling is the reason two speakers can leave a quiet patch in a room where their sounds arrive half a cycle apart, and it depends on the delay relative to the *period* of the tone.

diagram.alt: Two equal 250 hertz waves and their sum. In phase, the sum has twice the peak height. A quarter cycle apart, the sum has a peak of about 1.41. Half a cycle apart, the waves cancel and the sum is flat.
diagram.caption: Two equal tones and their sum. Use the buttons to move the second tone later by a fraction of a cycle.

reveal.text: In a room the delay comes from the extra path the sound takes: 2.5 ms at 343 m/s is about 0.86 m.

lessons.orientation: How frequency, period, wavelength and amplitude describe a repeating sound wave.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson shows that real sounds are not single repeating shapes but sums of many frequencies, and that this mixture is what gives an instrument its character.

blocks.text: A microphone records the pressure at one point as a sound passes, and what it draws is a line that rises and falls. A steady note makes that line repeat exactly, and two features of the repeat are easy to read off the page: how often it comes round, and how tall it is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between frequency, period and wavelength, and say which feature of a wave sets pitch and which sets loudness.
intro.whyItMatters: Pitch, bass and treble, and why low sounds bend round corners while high ones do not, all depend on these three quantities.

recap.keyIdea: A tone’s frequency sets its pitch and its period is 1 / f, its amplitude sets its loudness, and its wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency.

blocks.text: Each cycle of a tone takes a period T = 1 / f, so 250 Hz means 4 ms per cycle, and the pitch follows the frequency while the loudness follows the amplitude. A loud and a quiet 440 Hz tone therefore have one pitch.

Because every frequency travels at the same speed in a given medium, v = f × wavelength, so a higher frequency has a shorter wavelength: 17.15 m at 20 Hz and 0.78 m at 440 Hz. Two equal tones half a cycle apart cancel completely.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows that real sounds are not single repeating shapes but sums of many frequencies, and that this mixture is what gives an instrument its character.

lessons.title: Harmonics and timbre

reveal.text: The repeat rate and the peak height are already matched, so only the shape inside each cycle is left, and the next screen shows how that shape is described.

lead.text: In the figure both notes repeat every 1/220 s, so both are at 220 Hz, yet one trace is nearly smooth and the other jagged. The jagged one is not a different kind of wave. In 1822 Joseph Fourier showed, in his work on how heat spreads through solids, that a repeating shape can be written as a sum of sine waves, and for sound this means that any steady note is a sum of sines at whole-number multiples of its repeat rate. The lowest of these is the **fundamental**, and the whole set are the **harmonics**.

A plot that gives the amplitude of each component against its frequency is a **spectrum**, drawn beneath each waveform as a row of bars. The flute-like note is nearly all fundamental, while the violin-like note has strong bars right across the first eight harmonics.

afterFigure.text: The ear hears the pitch of both notes as 220 Hz, because pitch follows the fundamental, and the difference it hears between them is their **timbre**, the quality that separates two sounds of the same pitch and loudness. Timbre depends largely on how the amplitude is shared among the harmonics. Notice that the tallest bar in the violin-like spectrum is the second, not the first: the pitch is still set by the *fundamental*, even when a higher component is stronger.

diagram.alt: Two notes at the same pitch of 220 hertz. The flute-like waveform is nearly a smooth sine and its spectrum has one tall bar at harmonic 1 and two small ones. The violin-like waveform is jagged and its spectrum has eight bars, with harmonic 2 the tallest.
diagram.caption: The same pitch with two different shapes. Each waveform is drawn above the bars that make it up. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The tallest component is not always the one that sets the pitch, which is why the fundamental is defined by its position in the series and not by its size.

lead.text: The harmonics are numbered from the fundamental, which is the *first* harmonic, so the second harmonic is 2f, the third is 3f, and the nth is n × f. For a note of 220 Hz they fall at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on. The first overtone, the first component above the fundamental, is therefore the *second* harmonic, which is a source of frequent confusion.

afterFigure.text: The musical meaning of these numbers is that doubling the frequency raises a note by one octave, so 2f is an octave above the fundamental, and 3f is an octave and a fifth above it.

diagram.alt: Eight bars at whole-number multiples of the fundamental. For a 220 hertz note they are at 220, 440, 660, 880, 1,100, 1,320, 1,540 and 1,760 hertz, with heights falling as 1 over the harmonic number. For a 110 hertz note every frequency is halved.
diagram.caption: The harmonic series. Each bar sits at a whole-number multiple of the fundamental. Use the buttons to change the fundamental.

reveal.text: The harmonics of 130 Hz are 130, 260, 390, 520, 650 and 780 Hz, each one 130 Hz above the last.

lead.text: A **square wave** switches abruptly between a high and a low value, and it looks nothing like a sine, yet it can be built from sines. Its spectrum has only the *odd* harmonics, 1, 3, 5, 7 and so on, with amplitude 1/n for the nth, so for a 100 Hz square wave the components are 100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz with amplitudes 1, 1/3, 1/5 and 1/7. A **sawtooth** wave, which ramps up and then drops, has *all* the harmonics, again with amplitude 1/n.

afterFigure.text: Sharp corners need high harmonics, which is why a wave with sharp corners sounds bright.

diagram.alt: A square wave built by adding odd harmonics. One harmonic gives a plain sine. Adding the 300 hertz harmonic starts to flatten the top. With three harmonics the sum has flat-ish tops and steeper sides. With five harmonics it closely follows the dashed square wave, with small ripples at the corners.
diagram.caption: Adding harmonics 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 of a 100 Hz square wave, each with amplitude 1/n. Use the buttons to add terms.

steps.headline: List the first four components of an ideal 150 Hz square wave and find the frequency of the fourth.

workedSteps.text: A square wave has only odd harmonics, so the multipliers are 1, 3, 5, 7 and not 1, 2, 3, 4.
Multiply the first three multipliers by the fundamental, 150 Hz.
The amplitudes are 1/n for each harmonic n.
The fourth multiplier in the list is 7. Give the frequency of the fourth component.

steps.headline: A sawtooth wave has all its harmonics with amplitude 1/n. Find the amplitude of its 4th harmonic relative to the first.

workedSteps.text: All the harmonics are present, so the 4th harmonic is at 4 times the fundamental, and its amplitude follows the same 1/n rule.
Divide 1 by the harmonic number to give the amplitude relative to the first harmonic.

lead.text: A **pure sine** has a single line. An instrument note has a row of separate lines at the harmonics, and the pattern of their heights is its timbre. **Noise**, such as the hiss of a breath or a cymbal crash, has energy spread over a continuous band of frequencies, so there are no separate lines to count and no single pitch.

afterFigure.text: This is why the spectrum is so useful: it separates what a pure sine and a violin have in common, which is the pitch, from what makes them different.

diagram.alt: Three spectra from 0 to 2,000 hertz. A pure sine has a single line at 220 hertz. An instrument note has a row of separate lines at multiples of 220 hertz. Noise has a continuous band of energy with no separate lines.
diagram.caption: Spectra of three kinds of sound. Use the buttons to compare them.

lessons.orientation: How a sound is a sum of sines at harmonics of its frequency, and how its spectrum gives its timbre.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson asks where harmonics come from physically, by looking at the waves that fit on a string or in a pipe.

blocks.text: Play the same note on a flute and on a violin, at the same loudness, and anyone can tell which is which. Recorded by a microphone, the two pressure traces repeat at the same rate, and their peaks reach the same height, so whatever the ear uses to tell them apart must lie somewhere else in the trace.

Finding it means breaking each trace into simpler pieces, pure tones at whole-number multiples of the note's frequency, and the list of how strong each piece is, called the sound's spectrum, describes a sound more usefully than the trace itself. With it you can explain why a clarinet sounds hollow, why a wave with sharp corners sounds bright, and what a filter will take away.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the harmonics of a note, read a spectrum, and say what a square wave or a pure sine contains.
intro.whyItMatters: The spectrum is the main tool for describing a sound, and later lessons on filters, equalisers and compression act on it.

recap.keyIdea: A steady sound is a sum of sine waves at the harmonics f, 2f, 3f and so on, and the spectrum that shows their amplitudes is what gives a sound its timbre.

blocks.text: The harmonics of a note lie at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, and the pitch follows the fundamental even when a higher harmonic is stronger. How the amplitude is shared among the harmonics is the timbre: a square wave has the odd harmonics at 1/n, a sawtooth has all of them at 1/n, and a pure sine has just one.
Noise differs in kind from all of these, because its spectrum is continuous and so it has no fundamental and no single pitch.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks where harmonics come from physically, by looking at the waves that fit on a string or in a pipe.

lessons.title: Resonance and standing waves

reveal.text: A wave that fits its ends is the only kind that survives on the string, and the wavelength of 1.3 m turns the speed of the wave into a frequency.

lead.text: When a wave runs along a string it reflects at each fixed end and comes back, and the waves going in each direction add. Most of the time the sum is a muddle that fades, but for particular wavelengths the two add into a pattern that stays in place: a **standing wave**, with points that never move, called **nodes**, and points that move most, called **antinodes**. The ends are fixed, so each is a node, and the string must hold a whole number of half wavelengths, which means the wavelength can be 2L, or L, or 2L/3, and in general 2L / n.

afterFigure.text: Each allowed pattern is a **mode**, and the frequency follows from v = f × wavelength: f = v / (2L / n), which is **fₙ = n × v / (2L)**. The first mode is the fundamental and the rest are its harmonics, so the harmonic series of the previous lesson comes from this: a plucked string excites several modes at once, and the pattern of their sizes is its timbre. Here v is the speed of waves *along the string*, set by its tension and its mass per length, and not the speed of sound in air.

diagram.alt: A string fixed at both ends in its first four standing-wave modes. Mode 1 is one arch, half a wavelength. Mode 2 has two arches and a node in the middle, mode 3 has three arches and mode 4 has four. Nodes are marked with dots.
diagram.caption: The four lowest modes of a string. The length L always holds a whole number of half wavelengths. Use the buttons to change the mode.

reveal.text: Shortening a string, as a player does by pressing a finger on it, raises the frequency, because the same wave speed now fits shorter half wavelengths.

steps.headline: A string 0.65 m long carries waves at 260 m/s. Find its first three mode frequencies.

workedSteps.text: The nth mode has wavelength 2L / n, so the first has wavelength 2 × 0.65 = 1.3 m.
Divide the wave speed by that wavelength to give the frequency of the first mode.
The second mode has half the wavelength and so twice the frequency.
The third mode has a third of the wavelength. Give its frequency.

lead.text: Air in a pipe behaves in the same way, with waves reflecting from the ends. At an open end the air moves freely, so there is a displacement antinode there, and at a closed end the air cannot move, so there is a node. An **open pipe** therefore has an antinode at each end, and fits whole numbers of half wavelengths just as the string does: fₙ = n × v / (2L), for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. A **closed pipe**, closed at one end and open at the other, has a node at one end and an antinode at the other, and the shortest pattern that fits is a *quarter* of a wavelength.

afterFigure.text: The closed pipe can only hold an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so its frequencies are fₙ = n × v / (4L) with n = 1, 3, 5 and so on. Its lowest frequency is half that of an open pipe of the same length, an octave lower, and its even harmonics are missing.

diagram.alt: Two pipes with the displacement patterns of their first three modes. The open pipe has antinodes at both ends and its modes are f, 2f and 3f. The closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, and its modes are f, 3f and 5f.
diagram.caption: Displacement patterns in an ideal pipe. Use the buttons to switch between open and closed ends.

reveal.text: Organ builders use this relationship directly: each pipe is cut to a length that gives its note.

lead.text: The figure compares the frequencies of an ideal pipe 0.50 m long, in air at 343 m/s. Open at both ends, it has f₁ = 343 / (2 × 0.50) = 343 Hz and then 686, 1,029 Hz and so on. Closed at one end, it has f₁ = 343 / (4 × 0.50) = 171.5 Hz, followed by 514.5, 857.5 Hz and so on, which are 3, 5 and 7 times the fundamental. The closed pipe is lower and, because it lacks the even harmonics, has a hollower timbre.

afterFigure.text: This is the same spectrum pattern that a square wave has, and the clarinet, which behaves like a closed pipe, is the example used in the last lesson.

diagram.alt: Frequencies of an ideal 0.50 metre pipe. The open pipe sounds 343, 686, 1,029 hertz and so on. The pipe closed at one end sounds 171.5, 514.5, 857.5 hertz and so on, which is half the lowest frequency and only odd multiples.
diagram.caption: The frequencies one pipe length can produce. Bar heights only suggest that higher modes are weaker. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Find the first two resonances of an ideal pipe 0.25 m long, closed at one end, in air at 343 m/s.

workedSteps.text: Only odd multiples of a quarter wavelength fit, so the fundamental is v / (4L).
The next resonance is the third harmonic, since the second is missing.

lead.text: The modes found so far are the **natural frequencies** of the string or pipe, the frequencies at which it vibrates freely once disturbed. If something pushes on the system repeatedly at one of those frequencies, each push arrives just as the last has finished one cycle, so the pushes add and the vibration grows large. This is **resonance**. The figure plots how large the response is as the driving frequency changes, for a system with a natural frequency of 200 Hz.

afterFigure.text: How narrow the peak is depends on how quickly the system loses energy, called its damping: lightly damped systems, such as a wine glass, have a tall narrow peak, while heavily damped ones respond over a wide band.

diagram.alt: A response curve of a system with a natural frequency of 200 hertz. The response is small at low and high driving frequencies and peaks sharply near 200 hertz. With light damping the peak is tall and narrow, and with heavy damping it is lower and wider.
diagram.caption: Response of a system with one natural frequency of 200 Hz, driven at different frequencies. Use the buttons to change the damping.

reveal.text: The result is the lowest of the room modes, and the room reinforces any bass note near these frequencies, which is why bass notes are uneven from place to place in a small room.

lessons.orientation: How a wave fitting between two ends fixes the frequencies of a string or a pipe.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson follows sound into the ear, where the ear canal behaves as a pipe closed at one end.

blocks.text: A wine glass can be made to ring by running a wet finger round its rim, and a trained singer can shatter one by holding a note at exactly the right pitch. The glass does not respond equally to every pitch: it has a few frequencies at which a small push builds into a large vibration, and a string or a pipe has similar frequencies fixed by its length.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the lowest frequencies of a string or a pipe from its length and wave speed, and say why a closed pipe has only odd harmonics.
intro.whyItMatters: Instruments, rooms and the ear canal all depend on the same rule that a wave must fit between its reflecting ends.

recap.keyIdea: A wave that fits between reflecting ends forms a standing wave, giving a string or open pipe the frequencies n × v / (2L) and a closed pipe the odd frequencies n × v / (4L).

blocks.text: A string fixed at both ends, or a pipe open at both ends, holds whole numbers of half wavelengths and so has frequencies n × v / (2L), while a pipe closed at one end holds odd numbers of quarter wavelengths and has only the odd harmonics, at half the frequency. A string of 0.65 m with a wave speed of 260 m/s has a fundamental of 200 Hz, and a closed pipe of 0.50 m has one of 171.5 Hz.
Driven at one of these natural frequencies, a system responds strongly, and that effect is called resonance.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows sound into the ear, where the ear canal behaves as a pipe closed at one end.

lessons.title: How we hear

reveal.text: Counting doublings is how pitch intervals work, because the ear hears equal ratios as equal steps, and a later screen builds on it.

lead.text: The part of the ear you can see, the **pinna**, collects sound and guides it down the **ear canal** to the **eardrum**, a thin membrane that vibrates with the changing pressure. On the other side, in the middle ear, three small bones carry that vibration on: the **malleus**, which touches the eardrum, the **incus**, and the **stapes**, which touches the cochlea and is the smallest bone in the body. The chain of bones passes the eardrum’s vibration to the fluid-filled **cochlea**.

afterFigure.text: Inside the cochlea a stiff strip called the basilar membrane runs along its length, narrow and stiff at one end and wide and floppy at the other, so that each place along it responds most to one frequency. Rows of hair cells on the membrane convert its movement into nerve signals, and the position of the cells that fire tells the brain the pitch.

diagram.alt: A flow of five parts: pinna and ear canal, eardrum, the three small bones, the cochlea and the auditory nerve, grouped into outer, middle and inner ear. One group at a time is highlighted with a description of its job.
diagram.caption: The path of sound through the ear. Use the buttons to see what each part of the ear does.

reveal.text: The stapes is only a few millimetres long.

lead.text: The ear canal is open to the air at one end and closed at the other by the eardrum, which is exactly the shape of a closed pipe, so the formula from the last lesson applies: f = v / (4L). For a canal of length 2.5 cm, a quarter wavelength fits when the wavelength is 4 × 0.025 = 0.10 m, so the frequency is 343 / 0.10 = 3,430 Hz.

afterFigure.text: Sound near this frequency is reinforced by the canal, and this is part of the reason the ear is so sensitive between about 2 and 5 kHz.

diagram.alt: A pipe 2.5 centimetres long, open at the left and closed at the right by the eardrum. The pressure pattern has a quarter of a wavelength in the pipe, so the wavelength is 10 centimetres and the frequency 3,430 hertz.
diagram.caption: The ear canal modelled as an ideal pipe closed at the eardrum, so the canal holds a quarter of a wavelength.

reveal.text: This is part of the reason infants are more sensitive to higher frequencies than adults are.

steps.headline: An ear canal is 3.0 cm long. Find its lowest resonance, in air at 343 m/s.

workedSteps.text: The canal is closed at the eardrum, so the length is a quarter of a wavelength.
The frequency is the speed divided by the wavelength.
Work out the division and give the frequency to the nearest hertz.

lead.text: A microphone responds almost equally at every audible frequency, but the ear does not. If you play a 1,000 Hz tone at a fixed level and ask a listener to adjust a tone at another frequency until it sounds equally loud, the level needed depends strongly on the frequency, and the curve joining such levels is an **equal-loudness contour**. Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson published the first set in 1933, and the standard today is ISO 226, last revised in 2023. The figure is an approximate version for quiet sound, with the level in decibels, the scale that the next lesson explains.

afterFigure.text: The curve falls from near 100 at 20 Hz to 40 at 1,000 Hz, and its lowest point lies near 3,000 to 4,000 Hz, close to the canal’s resonance. At quiet levels a 50 Hz tone therefore needs tens of decibels more than a 3,000 Hz tone to sound as loud, which is why bass seems to disappear when music is played quietly.

diagram.alt: An equal-loudness curve on a logarithmic frequency axis. It sits near 100 decibels at 20 hertz, falls to 40 at 1,000 hertz, dips lowest near 3,000 to 4,000 hertz at about 34, and rises again towards 8,000 hertz.
diagram.caption: An approximate equal-loudness contour for quiet sound. The lower the curve, the less level the ear needs there.

lead.text: Raise a note by an octave and its frequency doubles, whether you start at 55 Hz or at 880 Hz. The two octaves from 55 Hz to 220 Hz span only 165 Hz, while the next two, from 220 Hz to 880 Hz, span 660 Hz, yet they sound like equal steps. The ear judges pitch by *ratios* of frequency.

afterFigure.text: The number of octaves between two frequencies is therefore the number of doublings in their ratio, which is the base-2 logarithm: octaves = log₂(f₂ / f₁). Across the audible range 20,000 / 20 = 1,000, and since 2¹⁰ = 1,024, the range is about 10 octaves.

diagram.alt: Five notes at 55, 110, 220, 440 and 880 hertz on a line. Spaced by frequency they crowd to the left. Spaced by pitch, which is how they are heard, they are evenly spaced, each step a doubling.
diagram.caption: The same five notes plotted two ways. Equal steps in pitch are equal ratios of frequency. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: How many octaves lie between 110 Hz and 3,520 Hz?

workedSteps.text: An octave is a doubling, so first find the ratio of the two frequencies.
Count how many doublings make 32.
The number of factors of 2 is the number of octaves.

steps.headline: A piano runs from 27.5 Hz to 4,186 Hz. How many octaves is that?

workedSteps.text: Find the ratio of the highest frequency to the lowest.
The number of octaves is the base-2 logarithm of that ratio, and a calculator can give it.

lead.text: The ten-octave range is a nominal figure for young ears.

reveal.text: Hearing loss usually begins at the top, which is why a listener may miss the high consonants of speech before missing any bass.

lessons.orientation: The path of sound through the ear, the canal’s resonance, the limits of hearing, and why pitch is heard as ratios.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson introduces the decibel, the logarithmic scale used for the levels that the equal-loudness curves are drawn in.

blocks.text: A sound reaches the ear as a tiny change of air pressure, at most a few thousandths of a percent of atmospheric pressure for everyday speech, and yet the ear turns it into a clear sense of pitch, loudness and direction. It does this with a short tube, a membrane, three bones smaller than a grain of rice and a fluid-filled coil, and each of these has a measurable effect on what reaches the brain.
Following a sound through these parts explains why bass seems to fade when music is played quietly and why the ear is most sensitive to frequencies of a few thousand hertz.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow sound through the ear, find the resonance of the ear canal, and count the octaves in a range of hearing.
intro.whyItMatters: Hearing is shaped by the ear, so what a recording needs to keep depends on what the ear can use.

recap.keyIdea: The ear passes vibration through the eardrum and three bones to the cochlea, its canal resonates near 3 kHz, and it hears equal frequency ratios as equal steps in pitch.

blocks.text: Sound passes along the ear canal, which resonates like a pipe closed at one end, to the eardrum, then through the malleus, incus and stapes to the cochlea, where each place on the basilar membrane responds to one frequency. A canal of 2.5 cm gives 3,430 Hz, in the band of greatest sensitivity.

The ear is not flat: equal-loudness contours show that tones of different frequency need different levels to sound equally loud, and it judges pitch by ratios, so the 20 to 20,000 Hz range of young ears is about 10 octaves.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson introduces the decibel, the logarithmic scale used for the levels that the equal-loudness curves are drawn in.

lessons.title: Decibels

reveal.text: A ratio of a million is awkward to write and to compare, which is the problem the decibel was introduced to solve.

lead.text: The ear works over an enormous range. The faintest sound it can detect has an intensity of about 1e-12 W/m², and a sound of about 1 W/m² is painful, a ratio of a million million. Numbers over that span are hard to handle, but a logarithm shrinks it. The base-10 logarithm of a number is the power of ten that gives it, so log₁₀(1,000) = 3 and log₁₀(1e12) = 12. The **decibel** (dB) takes this logarithm of the ratio of an intensity to a reference intensity and multiplies it by ten: level = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀).

afterFigure.text: In the figure each step of 10 dB along the axis is a factor of ten in intensity. A sound of 1e-6 W/m² against the reference of 1e-12 W/m² has a ratio of 1e6, so its level is 10 × 6 = 60 dB, and the whole range from threshold to pain fits into about 120 dB. A decibel is always a *ratio*, so a level in dB means nothing without the reference it is measured against.

diagram.alt: A horizontal axis of intensity from 1e-12 to 1 watt per square metre with the level in decibels from 0 to 120 marked at every tenth step. The threshold of hearing is at 0 dB, conversation at about 60 dB and the pain threshold at about 120 dB.
diagram.caption: Intensity and level on one axis. Each tick is a factor of ten in intensity and 10 dB in level.

lead.text: Microphones and the ear respond to pressure, so levels are more often found from pressure than from intensity. Intensity is proportional to the *square* of the pressure, so a pressure ratio of p / p₀ gives an intensity ratio of (p / p₀)², and the logarithm of a square is twice the logarithm: 10 log₁₀((p / p₀)²) = **20 log₁₀(p / p₀)**. The result is called the **sound pressure level**, or **SPL**, and it is quoted in dB SPL.

afterFigure.text: The reference pressure is p₀ = 20 micropascals, the nominal threshold of hearing at 1 kHz, so the threshold is 0 dB SPL, and a pressure of 2 Pa gives 20 log₁₀(2 / 0.00002) = 20 log₁₀(100,000) = 100 dB SPL. A level of 0 dB is therefore a reference and not silence.

lead.text: Two rules do most of the work in practice. If the power or intensity is doubled, the level rises by 10 log₁₀(2) = 3.01 dB, and if the pressure is doubled, it rises by 20 log₁₀(2) = 6.02 dB. The two are consistent, since doubling the pressure quadruples the power, and a factor of four in power is two doublings of 3.01 dB each.

afterFigure.text: Equal sources that are independent of one another add their *powers*, so two equal sources double the power and add 3.01 dB, not double the number of decibels. Two sources of 50 dB give 53 dB.

diagram.caption: The same multipliers give twice as many decibels for pressure as for power. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Two independent sources each produce 60 dB at your position. What level do they make together?

workedSteps.text: Independent sources add their powers, not their decibels, so the total power is twice that of one.
Doubling the power adds 10 log₁₀(2), which is 3.01 dB.
Add this to the level of one source, and give the total to one decimal place.

lead.text: A point source in open space spreads its power over a sphere, and the area of a sphere grows with the square of its radius, so the intensity falls as 1 / r², which is called the **inverse-square law**. Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to a quarter, which is two halvings of 3.01 dB, so the level falls by 6.02 dB. In general the change is 20 log₁₀(r₂ / r₁).

afterFigure.text: From 1 m to 8 m there are three doublings, so the level is 3 × 6.02 = 18.06 dB lower. The law applies only in free space, so in a room the level falls more slowly with distance than it should.

diagram.alt: Level against distance from a point source, relative to 1 metre. Each doubling of distance lowers the level by 6.02 decibels: 0 at 1 metre, minus 6.02 at 2 metres, minus 12.04 at 4, minus 18.06 at 8 and minus 24.08 at 16 metres.
diagram.caption: Level against distance. Each doubling of distance, drawn as equal steps, lowers the level by 6.02 dB.

reveal.text: A factor of ten in distance is 20 dB, so a source 10 m away is 20 dB quieter than at 1 m, and one at 100 m is 40 dB quieter.

steps.headline: A loudspeaker produces 90 dB at 1 m. Find its level at 4 m, treating it as a point source in free space.

workedSteps.text: The distance has doubled twice, from 1 m to 2 m and then to 4 m.
Each doubling lowers the level by 6.02 dB, so the total drop is 2 × 6.02.
Subtract the drop from 90 dB and give the level to the nearest whole number.

lead.text: Loud sound damages the hair cells of the cochlea, and the harm depends on both level and time. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends a limit of 85 dBA over an eight-hour day, where the A means the level has been weighted to follow the ear’s sensitivity. It uses an exchange rate of 3 dB: every increase of 3 dB doubles the energy reaching the ear each second, so the time allowed is halved.

afterFigure.text: The rule is T = 8 hours / 2^((L − 85) / 3). It sets a limit on the energy received over a day, so a short loud sound and a long quieter one can carry the same risk.

diagram.alt: Bars for the recommended daily exposure time at five levels: 8 hours at 85 dBA, 4 hours at 88, 2 hours at 91, 1 hour at 94 and 30 minutes at 97. Each 3 decibel increase halves the time.
diagram.caption: Recommended maximum daily exposure. Each increase of 3 dB halves the time allowed.

lessons.orientation: How the decibel turns ratios of intensity or pressure into additions, and what that gives for levels and distance.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson turns to digital audio, and how a continuous wave is measured at equal time steps.

blocks.text: The faintest sound an ear can detect has an intensity of about 1e-12 W/m², and a sound that hurts has about 1 W/m², a million million times more. A scale that is to describe both ends has either to write numbers with a dozen zeros or to count the zeros instead, and counting the zeros, which is what a logarithm does, is the idea behind the decibel.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between intensity or pressure ratios and decibels, and predict how the level changes when sources are added or the distance changes.
intro.whyItMatters: Levels in decibels appear in every part of audio, from microphone gain and loudness meters to hearing safety.

recap.keyIdea: A level in decibels is 10 log of an intensity ratio or 20 log of a pressure ratio, so doubling power adds 3 dB, doubling pressure or halving distance adds 6 dB, and sources add by their powers.

blocks.text: The decibel counts factors of ten: 10 dB for each tenfold change in intensity and 20 dB for each tenfold change in pressure, measured against a reference such as 20 µPa. Doubling the power adds 3.01 dB, so two 60 dB sources make 63 dB, and doubling the pressure adds 6.02 dB.
The inverse-square law makes each doubling of distance from a point source lower the level by 6.02 dB, and exposure guidance halves the time allowed for every 3 dB above 85 dBA.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to digital audio, and how a continuous wave is measured at equal time steps.

lessons.title: Sampling and aliasing

reveal.text: Forty-odd points on each cycle is plenty to trace the wave, and the next screen asks how few would be enough.

lead.text: A computer cannot store a continuous pressure curve, which has a value at every instant, so it measures the curve at equal steps of time and stores the measurements as numbers. This is **sampling**, each measurement is a **sample**, and the number of samples per second is the **sample rate**, written fs.

afterFigure.text: The theorem that tells you how few are enough is attributed to Nyquist and Shannon. A signal that contains no frequency at or above half the sample rate can be rebuilt *exactly* from its samples, by joining them with a smooth curve, which is not the staircase of steps that people often imagine. Half the sample rate is called the **Nyquist frequency**, so a rate of fs can represent frequencies below fs / 2. With exactly 2 samples per cycle the result depends on where the dots fall, and the last case in the figure places them on the zero crossings and records nothing, which is why the rate must be *more* than twice the frequency.

diagram.alt: A sine wave sampled at three rates. With 16 samples per cycle the dots trace the wave clearly. With 4 per cycle they still pin it down. With exactly 2 per cycle placed at the zero crossings, every sample is zero and the tone cannot be seen.
diagram.caption: One tone, three sample rates. The dots are the samples. Use the buttons to reduce the number of samples per cycle.

reveal.text: At 48,000 Hz everything below 24,000 Hz can be represented, with room above the 20,000 Hz limit of hearing.

lead.text: What happens to a tone that is *above* the Nyquist frequency? The figure samples a 900 Hz tone once every millisecond, so fs is 1,000 Hz and the Nyquist frequency is 500 Hz. The dots fall at one point in each millisecond, and a 100 Hz tone, with its sign flipped, passes through exactly the same dots, so after sampling the two tones cannot be told apart. The tone has **aliased**: it appears at a lower frequency, called its **alias**.

afterFigure.text: For a tone between the Nyquist frequency and the sample rate the alias is fs − f, which here is 1,000 − 900 = 100 Hz. The same happens at any rate: with fs = 44,100 Hz, a tone at 30,000 Hz appears at 44,100 − 30,000 = 14,100 Hz. The damage cannot be undone afterwards, since the folded tone is *indistinguishable* from a real tone at the lower frequency, so the only remedy is to stop the tone reaching the sampler.

diagram.alt: A 900 hertz sine wave sampled once every millisecond, shown with the samples as dots. A 100 hertz sine wave, with its sign flipped, passes through exactly the same dots. After sampling the two tones cannot be told apart.
diagram.caption: A tone above the Nyquist frequency and the lower tone with identical samples. Use the buttons to see each curve and then both.

reveal.text: An ultrasonic tone that nobody could hear becomes an audible one, which is why the filter below is needed.

steps.headline: A 26,000 Hz tone is sampled at 48,000 Hz with no filter. At what frequency does it appear?

workedSteps.text: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate.
The tone is above it, and below the sample rate, so it folds back.
The alias is the sample rate minus the tone. Work it out.

lead.text: Because aliasing cannot be repaired afterwards, an **anti-aliasing filter** is placed before the sampler. It is a low-pass filter, which passes the frequencies of interest and removes those above the Nyquist frequency, so there is nothing left to fold back.

afterFigure.text: A filter cannot cut off instantly, so it needs a margin between the highest wanted frequency and the Nyquist frequency. To capture 20,000 Hz the sample rate must exceed 40,000 Hz, and the standard rates of 44,100 and 48,000 Hz leave 2,050 and 4,000 Hz of room above 20,000 Hz for the filter to fall away. The figure of 44,100 Hz has a history: early digital audio was stored on video recorders, and three samples on each of 245 lines in each of 60 fields a second give 3 × 245 × 60 = 44,100, as 3 × 294 × 50 does for 50-field video.

diagram.alt: Spectra at a 44,100 hertz sample rate. Without a filter, a 30,000 hertz tone above the Nyquist frequency of 22,050 hertz folds back and appears at 14,100 hertz. With an anti-aliasing filter, the region above the Nyquist frequency is removed before sampling, so no alias appears.
diagram.caption: The effect of an anti-aliasing filter. Use the buttons to compare sampling with and without it.

steps.headline: What sample rate is needed to capture a 15,000 Hz tone?

workedSteps.text: The sample rate must be more than twice the highest frequency present.
Work out the limit that the sample rate must exceed.

lead.text: Harry Nyquist analysed the limits of telegraph signalling in 1928, and Claude Shannon gave the sampling theorem in its familiar form for communications in 1949. Neither was thinking of music, but the result applies to any signal, which is why one theorem governs audio, images and radio.

afterFigure.text: More samples above the Nyquist limit therefore add nothing: a tone below half the sample rate is already completely described by its samples, so raising the rate from 44,100 to 96,000 Hz does not add detail to a 5,000 Hz tone. What a higher rate does add is room above the audible range, which relaxes the filter.

reveal.text: A filter with its edge below 24,000 Hz would have removed it, and that is the job the anti-aliasing filter does.

lessons.orientation: How sampling measures a wave at equal steps, and what happens to a tone above half the sample rate.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson looks at the other half of digital audio: how many levels each sample can take, and how much data that makes.

blocks.text: A microphone produces a pressure that changes continuously, but a computer stores only lists of numbers, so something has to turn one into the other. The obvious way is to measure the pressure at regular instants, and the obvious worry is that the stretches between the measurements are lost. A surprising result, which Claude Shannon stated in 1949, says that nothing is lost provided the measurements come often enough.

The condition turns on two numbers, the sample rate and half of it, and knowing them lets you say which frequencies a recording made at 44,100 samples a second can hold, and at what lower frequency a tone that is too high for it will turn up instead.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the Nyquist frequency for a sample rate and predict the frequency at which a tone above it will appear.
intro.whyItMatters: Every digital recording is a list of samples, and the sample rate decides which frequencies it can hold.

recap.keyIdea: A signal with no frequency above half the sample rate can be rebuilt exactly from its samples, and a tone above that Nyquist frequency folds back to fs minus its frequency.

blocks.text: Sampling measures the wave fs times a second, and a signal containing nothing above fs / 2, the Nyquist frequency, is rebuilt exactly by joining the samples smoothly. At 44,100 Hz the Nyquist frequency is 22,050 Hz.
A tone above it aliases to fs − f, so 30,000 Hz appears at 14,100 Hz, and nothing afterwards can separate it from a real low tone, so an anti-aliasing filter removes such frequencies before sampling.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the other half of digital audio: how many levels each sample can take, and how much data that makes.

lessons.title: Bit depth and data

reveal.text: The count doubles with each digit, and that doubling is what the next screens use to find the dynamic range.

lead.text: Sampling fixes *when* the wave is measured, but each measurement must also be stored as a number, and a computer stores a number with a fixed count of binary digits, or **bits**. A sample of N bits can take 2ᴺ different values, so the true pressure has to be rounded to the nearest of 2ᴺ **levels**. This rounding is called **quantisation**, and N is the **bit depth**.

afterFigure.text: The errors are small compared with the whole wave and have no pattern that follows it, so the ear hears them as a faint hiss, the **quantisation noise**. Adding a bit doubles the number of levels, so it halves the spacing between them and halves the error. Bit depth does not touch the *frequency range*: that is set by the sample rate.

diagram.alt: A sine wave sampled and rounded to 3, 4 and 6 bits. With 3 bits there are 8 levels, shown as dashed lines, and the stored dots are visibly far from the true curve. With 4 bits there are 16 levels, and with 6 bits there are 64 and the rounding errors are small.
diagram.caption: The same wave stored with more and more levels. Each short orange mark is the rounding error of one sample. Use the buttons to add bits.

reveal.text: Early computers and games used 8-bit sound, with the noise that 256 levels give.

lead.text: The **dynamic range** is the gap between the loudest signal that can be stored and the quantisation noise that sits beneath it. Doubling the number of levels doubles the largest amplitude in comparison with the smallest step, and a doubling of amplitude is 6.02 dB, so each added bit buys about 6 dB. For an ideal quantiser and a full-scale sine wave the ratio of signal to quantisation noise is **6.02 N + 1.76 dB**.

afterFigure.text: For 16 bits this gives 6.02 × 16 + 1.76 = 98.08 dB, and 16 bits hold 2¹⁶ = 65,536 levels. For 24 bits the range is 146.2 dB and the levels number 16,777,216. It is tempting to think of 24 bits as 50% more than 16 because 24 is 50% more than 16, but each added bit *doubles* the levels, so 8 more bits give 256 times as many. The figure shows how the ideal range grows with bit depth, and real converters fall short of the ideal by several decibels.

diagram.alt: Bars for the ideal dynamic range at five bit depths: 8 bits give 49.9 decibels, 12 give 74.0, 16 give 98.1, 20 give 122.2 and 24 give 146.2. Each added bit adds about 6 decibels.
diagram.caption: Ideal dynamic range against bit depth, drawn to scale.

reveal.text: Two fewer bits than the 16 of a CD cost about 12 dB of range, which is part of why early digital recordings with fewer bits sound grainier.

lead.text: Every second of audio contains fs samples for each channel, and each sample takes N bits, so the **data rate** is fs × N × the number of channels. For CD audio, which uses 44,100 samples per second, 16 bits and 2 channels, this is 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, usually written 1,411.2 kbps. Dividing by 8 turns bits into bytes, so that is 176,400 bytes every second.

afterFigure.text: Multiplying by the duration gives the size: one minute of CD stereo is 176,400 × 60 = 10,584,000 bytes.

diagram.alt: Three multiplications of sample rate, bits per sample and channels. CD stereo: 44,100 by 16 by 2 gives 1,411,200 bits per second. A 48 kilohertz, 24-bit stereo recording gives 2,304,000. Telephone voice at 8,000 by 8 by 1 gives 64,000.

steps.headline: How many bytes does 30 seconds of 48,000 Hz, 24-bit stereo take?

workedSteps.text: A 24-bit sample takes 24 / 8 = 3 bytes, and there are two channels.
Multiply by the sample rate to find the bytes each second.
Multiply by the 30 seconds.

lead.text: The 2ᴺ levels cover a fixed range, and a signal that tries to go beyond the top level cannot be stored: the converter holds it at the limit. This is **clipping**. A flat-topped wave is no longer a pure sine, so its spectrum gains harmonics that were never in the original, and they are heard as harshness. Clipping is also permanent, since the information above the limit has been thrown away.

afterFigure.text: Quantisation error follows the signal when the signal is very small, and the ear can pick that pattern out as a gritty distortion. **Dither** adds a very small random noise before quantising, so that the error becomes an even, steady hiss.

diagram.alt: A sine wave inside the full-scale limits is unchanged. A sine whose peaks would reach 1.5 times full scale is flattened at the limits, so its tops are cut off.
diagram.caption: Clipping. Use the buttons to compare a signal inside the limits with one beyond them.

steps.headline: Find the data rate of uncompressed stereo audio at 96,000 Hz and 24 bits.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the sample rate by the bit depth to find the bits per second for one channel.
Now allow for the second channel, and give the total in bits per second.

lead.text: A signal does not have to fill the whole range, and a quiet recording uses only the lower levels.

reveal.text: This is why recordings should be made with the peaks near full scale, and why a quiet 16-bit file is noisier than it sounds on paper.

lessons.orientation: How many levels a bit depth gives, how that sets the dynamic range, and how much data uncompressed audio takes.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson shows how compressed formats store the same music in a fraction of this data, by using what the ear cannot hear.

blocks.text: A CD holds a little over 700 megabytes of music, and the number is no accident: it follows from two choices made for every sample. How often to measure the pressure was the subject of the last lesson, and the other choice is how finely to record each measurement, because a number stored with a fixed count of binary digits can only take a fixed number of values.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the levels a bit depth gives, find its ideal dynamic range, and work out the data rate and size of uncompressed audio.
intro.whyItMatters: Bit depth and sample rate decide how much storage a recording needs and how much noise it carries.

recap.keyIdea: N bits give 2ᴺ levels and about 6 dB of dynamic range per bit, and uncompressed audio takes fs × N × channels bits every second.

blocks.text: A sample stored with N bits can take 2ᴺ values, so 16 bits give 65,536 levels and an ideal dynamic range of 98.1 dB, about 6 dB for each bit. Bit depth sets dynamic range, while sample rate sets the frequency range.

Multiplying sample rate, bit depth and channels gives a data rate of 1,411,200 bits per second for CD audio, or 10,584,000 bytes a minute, and a signal beyond full scale is clipped, while a very small amount of dither hides the quantisation error.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how compressed formats store the same music in a fraction of this data, by using what the ear cannot hear.

lessons.title: Compression and masking

reveal.text: This is much less than the 10,584,000 bytes of CD audio, and the next screens explain what is given up to achieve it.

lead.text: Compression stores the same recording in fewer bits, and it comes in two kinds. **Lossless compression** finds a shorter way to write the *same* samples, as a zip file does for text, so that decoding returns an exact copy of the original, sample for sample. **Lossy compression** goes further and throws information away, choosing what to discard so that listeners are not expected to miss it, so the decoded signal is *not* identical to the original.

afterFigure.text: Lossless does not mean smaller than lossy: it usually means *larger*, since it must keep every sample, and a lossless file is typically around half of the uncompressed size. Lossy files can be a tenth or less.

diagram.alt: A chain of five boxes: original samples, encoder, smaller file, decoder, output samples. For lossless compression the output is identical to the original. For lossy compression the output differs, with detail discarded that listeners are not expected to miss.
diagram.caption: The two kinds of compression. Use the buttons to compare what comes out at the end of each.

reveal.text: A ratio of about 4.4 to 1 is mild for a lossy codec, which is why 320 kbps is often treated as near the top of the quality range.

lead.text: In silence the ear can detect a very quiet tone, and the dashed curve in the figure shows the quietest sound heard at each frequency. Now play a loud tone at 1,000 Hz. Near its frequency the ear is occupied by the loud tone, and the level a weaker tone needs before it can be heard rises sharply: the orange curve in the second case is the new threshold. Tone A, close to 1,000 Hz and at 40 dB, now lies under that curve and cannot be heard, although it is still in the air. Tone B, far above, is untouched.

afterFigure.text: This effect is called **masking**, and it works in time as well as frequency: a loud sound also hides weaker sounds in the instants just before it and just after it. The masked sound has not been removed from the pressure wave, but the listener cannot hear it, which makes it a candidate for deletion. The effect is stronger for frequencies *above* the loud one than for those below, so the curve in the figure falls more slowly on the high side.

diagram.alt: A graph of level against frequency. The dashed curve is the quietest sound heard in silence. In a quiet room a loud 1 kilohertz tone and two weaker tones, A near it and B far above it, are all heard. With the loud tone playing, the threshold rises sharply near 1 kilohertz, hiding tone A while tone B, far enough away, is still heard.
diagram.caption: Masking. Use the buttons to compare the threshold in silence with the raised threshold around a loud tone.

reveal.text: The same effect is why a quiet conversation is hard to follow next to a running engine.

lead.text: A lossy codec such as MP3 splits the sound into short slices and frequency bands and estimates, for each slice, the masking threshold that the loud components create. In any band where the threshold is high, the quantisation noise from the last lesson can be larger without being heard, so the codec uses fewer bits for that band, and in a band where nothing is masked it spends more.

afterFigure.text: Equal sharing wastes bits on masked bands, while sharing by what is audible uses about half as many in total. The codec does not simply remove the high frequencies, as people often suppose: it follows the sound moment by moment, and a codec at a sensible **bitrate**, the data per second of the stored stream, gives a result that is transparent, meaning indistinguishable from the original for most listeners.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts of bits spent on eight frequency bands. With equal allocation each band gets 8 bits, 64 in total. With allocation that follows what is audible, bands where the sound is masked get few bits and the total is 33.
diagram.caption: Bits spent on each band for one short slice of sound, with and without a masking model. The numbers are illustrative.

steps.headline: By what ratio is CD audio larger than a stream at 256 kbps?

workedSteps.text: The CD data rate is 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, which is 1,411.2 kbps.
The compression ratio is the larger rate divided by the smaller, so divide by 256.
Work out the division and give it to two decimal places.

steps.headline: How many bytes does a 4-minute stream at 192 kbps take?

workedSteps.text: Four minutes is 240 seconds, and 192 kbps is 192,000 bits per second.
Divide by 8 to give bytes, and give the total.

lead.text: The sensible division of labour is that lossless formats such as FLAC suit an archive, where the exact samples must survive, and lossy formats such as MP3, AAC and Ogg Vorbis suit listening and streaming, where size matters and the missing detail goes unheard.

afterFigure.text: The codec decides what to discard from the signal it is given, and if that signal is already the output of a lossy codec, a second encode discards more, and a third more again, which is **generation loss**. Masters that will be edited again should therefore stay uncompressed or lossless.

diagram.alt: Bars for the size of a 3-minute stereo track. Uncompressed CD quality is 31.75 megabytes. A lossless file is typically about half, around 16 megabytes. A 320 kilobit per second lossy file is 7.2 megabytes and a 128 kilobit per second file is 2.88 megabytes.
diagram.caption: Sizes of one track in four forms. The lossless size is a typical figure and varies with the music.
