lessons.orientation: What lossless and lossy compression do, how masking makes lossy compression work, and how to compute ratios and sizes.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson turns from storing sound to shaping it, starting with how a compressor controls the dynamics of a signal.

blocks.text: A CD stores 1,411,200 bits for every second of stereo music, and a streaming service sends the same music at a tenth of that. The listener who plays both rarely hears a difference, even though most of the data has gone.

Much of that detail goes unheard because a loud sound makes the ear insensitive, for a moment, to quieter sounds close to it in frequency. A codec, the software that encodes sound into a compressed file and decodes it for playback, can estimate which sounds are hidden in each fraction of a second and spend its bits only where they will be heard.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell lossless from lossy compression, explain how masking lets a codec discard data, and work out compression ratios and stream sizes.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost all the music you hear is compressed, so it helps to know what has been kept and what has been thrown away.

recap.keyIdea: Lossless compression returns the exact samples, and lossy compression discards what masking hides from the listener, so a bitrate sets the size directly.

blocks.text: Lossless compression stores the same samples in fewer bits and decodes exactly, while lossy compression, by estimating what masking hides in each slice of sound, spends fewer bits where the error would not be heard. A loud sound raises the hearing threshold near its own frequency, and just before and after it, so weaker sounds there can be dropped.

At a given bitrate the stream size is the bitrate times the duration over eight, so 128 kbps for three minutes is 2,880,000 bytes, about an eleventh of CD audio at a ratio of 11 to 1, and each further lossy encode discards more.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from storing sound to shaping it, starting with how a compressor controls the dynamics of a signal.

lessons.title: Dynamics and compression

reveal.text: The ratio compares how much the input changes with how much the output changes, as the next screens set out.

lead.text: A note does not switch on at full level and stay there. Its amplitude follows a shape in time called its **envelope**, and the usual description has four parts. The **attack** is the rise from silence to the peak, the **decay** is the fall from the peak to a steady level, the **sustain** is the level held while the note is kept going, and the **release** is the fall to silence after it ends.

afterFigure.text: A struck or plucked sound, such as a drum or a guitar string, has a very short attack and then dies away by itself, so it has a decay and no true sustain. A held note, such as a bowed string or an organ pipe, stays at its sustain level for as long as the player keeps it going.

diagram.alt: Two amplitude envelopes. A plucked or struck sound rises quickly in an attack and then fades away in a long decay. A held note has four parts: attack to the peak, decay to a steady level, sustain while the note is held, and release after it ends.
diagram.caption: Envelopes of two kinds of sound. Use the buttons to compare a struck sound with a held note.

reveal.text: A quick attack gives a sound its percussive edge, and cutting it off removes much of what identifies a drum.

lead.text: A **compressor** turns down the loud parts of a signal and leaves the quiet parts alone, which narrows the gap between them. Two settings define it. The **threshold** T is the level above which it acts, and the **ratio** R says how strongly: for a ratio of 4:1, every 4 dB by which the input exceeds the threshold becomes 1 dB at the output. The ratio compares changes in level, so it is not itself measured in decibels.

afterFigure.text: Below the threshold the output equals the input, and above it the output is **T + (input − T) / R**. The figure plots that rule as a bend in a line: at 1:1 the line is straight, and the higher the ratio, the flatter the line above the threshold. A **limiter** is a compressor with a very high ratio, such as 20:1 or more, which makes the line almost flat so that the level cannot rise much above the ceiling set by the threshold.

diagram.alt: Input level against output level for a compressor with a threshold of minus 20 decibels. At 1 to 1 the output equals the input. At 2 to 1 an input of 0 gives minus 10, at 4 to 1 it gives minus 15, and a limiter at 20 to 1 gives about minus 19, almost flat above the threshold.
diagram.caption: The compressor transfer curve. Use the buttons to change the ratio and watch the slope above the threshold.

reveal.text: Only the part above the threshold is reduced; everything beneath −24 dB would pass unchanged.

steps.headline: A compressor has a threshold of −30 dB and a ratio of 5:1. Find the output and the gain reduction for an input of −10 dB.

workedSteps.text: The input is above the threshold by −10 − (−30) = 20 dB.
The output rises by the excess divided by the ratio, and that is added to the threshold.
The gain reduction is the input level minus the output level. Work it out.

lead.text: A real compressor cannot change its gain instantly without distorting the wave, so it has an **attack** time, which is how quickly it turns down once the level passes the threshold, and a **release** time, which is how quickly it lets go afterwards. The figure shows a loud burst through a 4:1 compressor. With a fast attack the output drops almost at once, while with a slow attack the start of the burst passes through before the gain comes down, which keeps the sharp front of a drum hit.

afterFigure.text: The amount taken off is the **gain reduction**, the input level minus the output level in dB, and here it is up to 9 dB. Turning down the loud parts leaves the whole signal quieter, so a compressor is usually followed by **makeup gain**, which raises everything by a fixed number of decibels. The result is that the quiet parts have been brought up and the loud parts held back, which is how compression makes a sound seem louder and more even without raising its peaks.

diagram.alt: Level against time for a burst of loud sound through a 4 to 1 compressor with a threshold of minus 20 decibels. With a fast attack the output drops to near its final level almost at once. With a slow attack the first part of the burst passes through before the gain comes down.
diagram.caption: Input and output levels for a loud burst. Use the buttons to change the attack time.

steps.headline: A compressor has a threshold of −12 dB and a ratio of 3:1. Find the gain reduction for an input of 0 dB.

workedSteps.text: The input is 12 dB above the threshold, so the output is the threshold plus 12 / 3.
The gain reduction is the input minus the output. Work it out.

lead.text: Two signals can have the same peak level and very different loudness, because the ear responds to the level over time and not to the highest instant. A limiter lets an engineer push the quiet parts up until the peaks touch the ceiling, which raises the loudness without raising the peak.

afterFigure.text: Loudness is therefore measured separately, in **LUFS**, a level weighted to follow the ear’s sensitivity and averaged over the whole programme. The European Broadcasting Union’s recommendation R 128 sets a target programme loudness of −23 LUFS for broadcast, and streaming services normalise to similar targets, so a recording made as loud as possible gains nothing and loses its dynamic range. Digital levels are given in **dBFS**, decibels relative to full scale, the highest level a converter can store.

diagram.alt: Two sounds drawn as bars of level over time, with the same peak. The first has a few sharp peaks and is otherwise low, so it is heard as quieter. The second stays near its peak, so it is heard as much louder.
diagram.caption: Two sounds with equal peaks and different loudness. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: The final peak is lower than the input peak by 3 dB, but every quiet part is 6 dB louder, which is the usual trade.

lessons.orientation: How an envelope describes a sound in time, and how a compressor maps input levels to output levels.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson changes the sound by frequency instead of by level, with filters and equalisers.

blocks.text: A drummer hits a snare at several levels in one bar, and the recording of it shows peaks that stand far above the quiet passages around them. If the whole recording is played loud enough to hear the quiet passages, the peaks are uncomfortable, and if it is played at a level that suits the peaks, the quiet passages disappear. The gap between the two is the dynamic range of the sound, and a compressor is the standard tool for narrowing it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate a compressor's output level and gain reduction, and describe the envelope of a sound.
intro.whyItMatters: Compressors and limiters sit in almost every recording and broadcast chain, so their settings are worth reading.

recap.keyIdea: A compressor lets the output rise by 1 dB for every R dB of input above its threshold, so the gain reduction is the input minus the output.

blocks.text: Above the threshold T a compressor gives output = T + (input − T) / R, so with a threshold of −20 dB and a ratio of 4:1 an input of −8 dB comes out at −17 dB, a gain reduction of 9 dB. A limiter is the same device with a very high ratio, and makeup gain raises the whole signal afterwards.

Attack and release times set how fast the gain follows the input, and because loudness depends on level over time and not on peaks alone, programmes are compared in LUFS, with broadcast aiming at −23.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson changes the sound by frequency instead of by level, with filters and equalisers.

lessons.title: EQ and filters

reveal.text: A filter’s slope is counted per octave, so counting octaves is the first step in every calculation that follows.

lead.text: A **filter** changes a sound by changing the level of each frequency by a different amount, and it is described by its **frequency response**, the gain it gives at each frequency, usually plotted in decibels. A **low-pass** filter passes frequencies below a chosen cutoff and reduces those above it, and a **high-pass** filter does the opposite. A **band-pass** filter passes a band around its centre and reduces what lies on either side. A **shelf** neither removes nor isolates anything, but raises or lowers *everything* above or below a corner frequency by a fixed amount.

afterFigure.text: Low-pass and high-pass filters are the tools for removing unwanted extremes, such as hiss or rumble, and shelves are what the bass and treble controls on an amplifier do. An equaliser, or EQ, is a set of such filters whose gains can be set.

diagram.alt: Four frequency responses on a logarithmic axis, level in decibels against frequency. A low-pass filter is flat at low frequencies and falls above its cutoff. A high-pass filter does the opposite. A band-pass filter peaks around its centre. A high shelf is flat low down and rises to a higher level above its corner.
diagram.caption: The shape of four common filters. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: Its mirror image is the high-pass filter, which is used to take rumble out of a recording.

lead.text: A filter does not switch a frequency off at its cutoff. The **cutoff frequency** is the point at which the response has fallen 3 dB from its level in the passband, and beyond it the signal fades gradually. How quickly it fades is the **slope**, in decibels per octave. Each added order of a simple filter adds about 6 dB per octave, so a first-order filter has 6 dB per octave, a second-order one 12 and a fourth-order one 24.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three low-pass filters with the same cutoff of 1,000 Hz. Two octaves above it, at 4,000 Hz, the 12 dB per octave filter is about 2 × 12 = 24 dB down, and the steeper one about 48 dB. A simple circuit gives the first-order case: an RC low-pass with R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF has a cutoff of fc = 1 / (2πRC), which is 995 Hz. The count of octaves matters, not the count of hertz: from 125 Hz to 1,000 Hz is 3 octaves, since each doubling is one.

diagram.alt: Low-pass responses with a cutoff of 1,000 hertz and slopes of 6, 12 and 24 decibels per octave. At the cutoff the level is 3 decibels down. Two octaves above, at 4,000 hertz, the level is about 12, 24 and 48 decibels down.
diagram.caption: Three slopes with the same cutoff. The dots are one octave apart. Use the buttons to steepen the slope.

reveal.text: Ignoring the 3 dB at the cutoff is the usual approximation once a tone is an octave or more beyond it.

steps.headline: A high-pass filter has a cutoff of 120 Hz and a slope of 18 dB per octave. How much is a 15 Hz rumble reduced?

workedSteps.text: Count the octaves between the rumble and the cutoff: 15 × 2 = 30, 30 × 2 = 60 and 60 × 2 = 120.
The attenuation is the slope times the number of octaves.
Work out the attenuation in decibels.

lead.text: A band-pass filter, or a bell-shaped boost or cut on an equaliser, has a centre frequency and a width. The **bandwidth** is the width of the band between the points where the response is 3 dB down, and the **Q factor** compares it with the centre: Q = centre frequency / bandwidth. A band centred on 1,000 Hz with a bandwidth of 250 Hz has a Q of 1,000 / 250 = 4.

afterFigure.text: A high Q means a narrow band. Q is a *ratio*, so the same Q means a wider band in hertz at 3,000 Hz than at 300 Hz.

diagram.alt: Three band-pass responses centred on 1,000 hertz. With a Q of 1 the band is 1,000 hertz wide between the minus 3 decibel points, with a Q of 4 it is 250 hertz wide, and with a Q of 10 it is 100 hertz wide.
diagram.caption: Bandwidth shrinks as Q rises. The green bar marks the band between the −3 dB points. Use the buttons to change Q.

reveal.text: A band this narrow is the kind used to notch out a single hum or ring.

steps.headline: A band is centred on 3,000 Hz and has a Q of 3. What is its bandwidth?

workedSteps.text: Rearrange Q = centre / bandwidth, so the bandwidth is the centre divided by Q.
Work out the division and give the bandwidth in hertz.

lead.text: **Equalisation** is the use of filters to change the balance of frequencies. In correcting a sound, a high-pass filter at about 80 Hz removes rumble that carries energy but no music, a cut near 250 Hz clears a muddy build-up, and a boost near 3 kHz, where hearing is most sensitive, brings out presence and the consonants of speech.

afterFigure.text: *Cutting* is often cleaner than boosting, because a boost raises the noise in that band and uses up headroom, with the risk of clipping, while a cut does neither.

diagram.alt: A frequency response with a high-pass cutoff at 80 hertz removing rumble, a cut of 4 decibels centred on 250 hertz, and a boost of 3 decibels centred on 3,000 hertz.
diagram.caption: A typical corrective EQ: cut the rumble, trim the muddy region, add a little presence.

reveal.text: A smaller capacitor raises the cutoff, so the circuit lets more of the treble through.

lessons.orientation: What low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and shelf filters do, and how slope and Q are calculated.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson turns from frequency to space, and shows how reflections in a room add reverberation to a sound.

blocks.text: A recording made in a room often carries a low rumble from traffic that no one hears directly, a muddy build-up in the middle of the spectrum, and a dullness at the top. Each of these is a matter of too much or too little at some frequency, and each can be treated by changing the level of that part of the spectrum alone.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the main filter types, work out the attenuation a slope gives, and find the Q of a band from its bandwidth.
intro.whyItMatters: Equalisers and filters are the most used tools in mixing, and their controls make sense once you can read a response.

recap.keyIdea: A filter reduces some frequencies, its cutoff is the 3 dB point, its slope is dB per octave and its Q is centre frequency divided by bandwidth.

blocks.text: A filter’s cutoff is the point where its response is 3 dB down, and beyond it the level falls by its slope, about 6 dB per octave for each order, so a 12 dB per octave low-pass at 1,000 Hz is 24 dB down at 4,000 Hz. A band is described by its centre and its Q, the centre divided by the bandwidth, so 1,000 Hz with 250 Hz of bandwidth has a Q of 4.
Equalisation applies these filters to correct a sound or make room in a mix, and cutting is often cleaner than boosting.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from frequency to space, and shows how reflections in a room add reverberation to a sound.

lessons.title: Reverb and space

reveal.text: The delay of 50 ms turns out to mark a boundary in how the ear treats reflections, which the later screens explain.

lead.text: Clap your hands in a large hall and three things reach you in order. First comes the **direct sound**, which travels in a straight line and arrives soonest. Then come a few separate **early reflections**, from the nearest walls, floor and ceiling. Last comes a dense tail, in which so many reflections arrive so close together that they no longer sound separate, and the combination is called **reverberation**. An echo is different: it is a single distinct repeat, heard as a separate event.

afterFigure.text: In the small room the early reflections come within a few milliseconds and the tail dies away quickly, and in the hall they come later and the tail is long, which is why a hall sounds large.

diagram.alt: Bars for sound arriving over time after a clap. The direct sound comes first. Then come a few separate early reflections, then a dense tail of many reflections that decays. In the large hall the early reflections arrive later and the tail lasts longer than in the small room.
diagram.caption: Arrivals at the listener after a clap, drawn as bars of level. Use the buttons to compare a small room and a large hall.

reveal.text: A cathedral has a long tail and a padded studio almost none, which is much of what makes the two sound so different.

lead.text: The tail of a room fades at a steady rate in decibels, so on a graph of level in dB against time it is close to a straight line. How long the tail lasts is measured by the **RT60**, the time it takes for the level to fall by 60 dB after the source stops. A fall of 60 dB is to a thousandth of the pressure, which is faint but not zero, so RT60 is not the time until silence.

afterFigure.text: Because the decay is straight, the level falls by 30 dB in half the RT60 and by 20 dB in a third of it. Different uses want different values: speech needs a short RT60 so that syllables do not smear into each other, while organ music is at home with a long one.

diagram.alt: A straight line of falling level against time after a source stops. It reaches minus 60 decibels at 0.5 seconds in one case and at 2.0 seconds in the other, and that time is the RT60.
diagram.caption: The decay of sound in a room, with level in decibels. The RT60 is the time to fall by 60 dB. Use the buttons to compare a short and a long decay.

reveal.text: The decay is a straight line in decibels, so equal times give equal falls.

lead.text: Around 1900 Wallace Clement Sabine, a physicist at Harvard, measured how long sound lasted in lecture rooms and found how it depended on the room. His result, in metric units, is **RT60 = 0.161 V / A** seconds, where V is the volume of the room in cubic metres and A is the **total absorption** in square metres, called sabins. The absorption is the area of each surface multiplied by how much of the sound it absorbs, added over all the surfaces.

afterFigure.text: For a room of 240 m³ with total absorption of 40 sabins, RT60 = 0.161 × 240 / 40 = 0.97 s. A larger volume lengthens the decay, since the sound has further to travel between reflections, and more absorption shortens it, so carpet and curtains halve it in the figure. The formula describes a room whose reflections are spread evenly, and it is least reliable in very dry rooms. More absorption is not always better: a very dry room lacks the cues that make a source sound present.

diagram.alt: A room of 240 cubic metres with total absorption of 40 sabins has an RT60 of 0.97 seconds. With carpet and curtains the absorption is 80 sabins and the RT60 halves to 0.48 seconds.
diagram.caption: The Sabine formula applied to one room before and after adding soft surfaces. Use the buttons to compare.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula, with V in cubic metres and A in sabins.
Substitute the volume and the absorption.
Work out the product, divide, and give the RT60 in seconds to two decimal places.

lead.text: The delay of a reflection follows from the speed of sound: the extra distance it travels, divided by 343 m/s. In the figure a source and a listener are 8 m apart, and a wall reflects the sound. With the wall 3 m from their line, the reflected path is two lengths of 5 m, which is 10 m, so it is 2 m longer than the direct path and arrives 2 / 343 = 5.8 ms later. With the wall at 7.5 m the path is 17 m and the reflection is 9 m longer, which is 26.2 ms later.

afterFigure.text: Reflections within about 50 ms, which is 17.15 m of extra path, fuse with the direct sound and make it fuller. For two similar sounds arriving a few milliseconds to about 30 ms apart, the ear does not hear two sources but places the sound where the *first* one came from, which is the **precedence effect**. A reflection later than that is heard as a separate echo.

diagram.alt: A plan view of a source and a listener 8 metres apart with a reflecting wall. With the wall 3 metres from their line the reflected path is 10 metres, 2 metres longer than the direct path, and arrives 5.8 milliseconds later. With the wall 7.5 metres away the reflected path is 17 metres and arrives 26.2 milliseconds later.
diagram.caption: How a reflection from a wall arrives later than the direct sound. Use the buttons to move the wall.

lead.text: In a room the direct sound falls with distance, by 6 dB for each doubling, as the inverse-square law requires, but the reverberant tail is made from reflections from every surface and stays at about the same level wherever you stand. Close to the source the direct sound dominates, and far from it the reverberation dominates, so the ratio between them changes steadily with distance.

afterFigure.text: The figure uses illustrative levels, with the two equal at about 8 m. Within that distance the source sounds near, and beyond it sounds far, though the total level changes little. A sound engineer treats the ratio of direct to reverberant sound as a control for distance.

diagram.alt: Level against distance for two parts of a sound in a room. The direct sound falls by 6 decibels for each doubling of distance, while the reverberant sound stays about level. They are equal at about 8 metres, and beyond that the reverberant sound dominates.
diagram.caption: Direct and reverberant levels against distance, with illustrative numbers. The ratio between them tells the ear how far away a source is.

steps.headline: A room of 300 m³ is to have an RT60 of 0.6 s. How much absorption does it need?

workedSteps.text: Rearrange RT60 = 0.161 V / A, so that the absorption is 0.161 V divided by RT60.
Work out the answer, in sabins.

reveal.text: Doubling the absorption halves the RT60, which is why a few soft furnishings change how a room sounds.

lessons.orientation: How reflections build reverberation, how long it lasts, and how late a reflection arrives.
lessons.nextAction: The last lesson uses all of this to design a sound, with layers, changes of speed, distance and movement.

blocks.text: In a bathroom a voice sounds rich and a little ringing, and in a field the same voice sounds thin and close. The words are the same, so the difference lies in what the surroundings do to the sound after it leaves the mouth: in the bathroom each wall sends back a copy that arrives a few milliseconds late, and the copies pile up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate a room's RT60 with Sabine's formula and convert the extra path of a reflection into a delay.
intro.whyItMatters: Reverberation is what makes a recording sound as though it was made in a particular space, and it is one of the main tools for placing a sound.

recap.keyIdea: Reverberation is many blended reflections, its decay is measured by RT60 = 0.161 V / A, and a reflection arrives later by its extra path divided by 343 m/s.

blocks.text: Reverberation is the persistence of sound made of many reflections, and its length is measured by the RT60, the time for the level to fall by 60 dB. Sabine’s formula, RT60 = 0.161 V / A, gives 0.97 s for 240 m³ and 40 sabins, and doubling the absorption halves it.

A reflection with an extra path of d arrives d / 343 s later, so 10 m gives 29.2 ms. Within about 50 ms it fuses with the direct sound, and the ratio of direct to reverberant sound is a cue for distance.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson uses all of this to design a sound, with layers, changes of speed, distance and movement.

lessons.title: Principles of sound design

reveal.text: Faster playback shortens a sound by the same factor that it raises the frequencies, which the next screen shows.

lead.text: A recording is a list of samples played at a fixed rate, and if you play the same samples faster, by a **playback ratio** r, every cycle takes 1 / r of the time, so every frequency is multiplied by r and the whole sound lasts 1 / r as long. Pitch and duration are locked together: a 3.0 s sample at 220 Hz played at ratio 2 lasts 1.5 s and sounds at 440 Hz, an octave higher, and the figure shows the same six cycles taking half the space.

afterFigure.text: Musical intervals set the ratio. An octave is 12 **semitones** and doubles the frequency, so each semitone is a factor of 2^(1/12), and n semitones is a ratio of **2^(n / 12)**. Five semitones up is 2^(5/12) = 1.335, which shortens the sample to 3.0 / 1.335 = 2.25 s and raises 220 Hz to 293.7 Hz. Changing pitch without length, or length without pitch, needs processing of the audio itself and cannot be done by changing the playback speed alone.

diagram.alt: A 3.0 second sample at 220 hertz, and the same sample played at a higher ratio. At ratio 2, 12 semitones up, it lasts 1.5 seconds and sounds at 440 hertz. At ratio 1.335, 5 semitones up, it lasts 2.25 seconds and sounds at 293.7 hertz. Duration and pitch change together.
diagram.caption: One sample played at three speeds. The six drawn cycles are the same, and only the time they take changes. Use the buttons to change the ratio.

reveal.text: A ratio of 1.498 is within a fraction of a per cent of 3:2, which is why seven semitones form a pleasing interval.

lead.text: A door slam, for example, is made from three parts. The **transient** is the short, sharp click at the start, which sits high in the spectrum, at about 2 to 8 kHz. The *body* is the wooden thud, in the region of 150 to 800 Hz, and the low tail is the room’s rumble, below about 100 Hz, which lasts longest. Building the sound in **layers** lets each part be chosen, filtered and timed separately.

afterFigure.text: Because the layers occupy different ranges, they do not mask one another, and the EQ of the lesson on filters is what keeps each in its range: a high-pass filter removes the low content from the click, and a low-pass filter trims the tail.

diagram.alt: A chart of frequency against time for a door slam built from three layers. A click occupies 2 to 8 kilohertz for about 0.1 seconds. A body of wood thud occupies 150 to 800 hertz for about 0.45 seconds. A low tail occupies 30 to 100 hertz and lasts about 1.5 seconds.
diagram.caption: Three layers, each in its own range of frequency and time. Layers that occupy different ranges do not hide one another.

lead.text: Three cues tell the ear that a sound is far away, and all three follow from earlier lessons. The direct sound is **quieter**, because its level falls by 6 dB for each doubling of distance. It is **duller**, because air absorbs high frequencies more than low ones over a long path. And it is **more reverberant** compared with the direct sound, because the reverberation stays at the same level while the direct sound falls.

afterFigure.text: A designer can place a sound at any distance by combining them: lower the level, reduce the highs with a low-pass filter, and raise the reverberation. A single cue is weak by itself, since a quiet sound may simply be soft, but together they are convincing.

diagram.alt: Three bars for a near sound and a far sound. A near sound is loud, bright and mostly direct. A far sound is quieter, duller because air absorbs highs, and has more reverberation compared with the direct sound.
diagram.caption: The three main cues for distance. Use the buttons to move the sound near and far.

lead.text: When a source of sound moves towards a listener, each crest it emits starts from a point nearer than the last, so the crests arrive closer together and the pitch is higher. When it moves away, they arrive further apart and the pitch is lower. This is the **Doppler shift**, and in the figure the circles are the crests, bunched ahead of the moving source and spread behind it. The speed is exaggerated, since a real car moves at a small fraction of the speed of sound.

afterFigure.text: For a source of frequency f moving at speed vs, with the speed of sound v, the frequency heard when it approaches is **f × v / (v − vs)** and when it recedes is **f × v / (v + vs)**. A 440 Hz horn approaching at 20 m/s is heard at 440 × 343 / 323 = 467 Hz, and at 440 × 343 / 363 = 416 Hz as it recedes. The shift depends on the relative velocity and not on the loudness, so it is the same for a quiet sound as for a loud one.

diagram.alt: Circles showing the crests of sound waves emitted by a source. For a source at rest the circles are concentric and evenly spaced. For a source moving to the right the circles are bunched closer together ahead of it and spread further apart behind it, so a listener ahead hears a higher pitch.
diagram.caption: Wave crests from a source at rest and from a moving source, with the speed exaggerated. Use the buttons to compare.

On the way out, the car recedes, so the denominator is v + vs.
Work out the division and give the frequency heard as the car moves away, in hertz.

workedSteps.text: Lowering by 5 semitones uses a ratio below 1.
Divide the duration by the ratio, and give the new length in seconds to two decimals.

lead.text: Every technique so far serves a purpose, and a designer starts from what a sound has to say. Sounds that belong to the story world, such as footsteps, a door slam or a voice in the scene, are called **diegetic**. Sounds that do not belong to it, such as a score or a narrator, are called **non-diegetic**, and they are heard by the audience but not by the characters.

afterFigure.text: The distinction matters because the two kinds are treated differently: a diegetic sound is placed in the space, with distance cues, reverberation and Doppler, so that it seems to come from somewhere, while a score sits outside the space and is not placed.

diagram.alt: Two groups of sound. Diegetic sounds belong to the story world, such as footsteps, a door slam and a voice in the scene. Non-diegetic sounds do not, such as the score, a narrator and interface sounds.
diagram.caption: Where a sound comes from decides how it is treated: a sound inside the story, and a sound outside it.
